This, but unironically

It’s tough to target these interventions because we know a lot less about our social-stats than we do about our food-stats and hydro-stats. We don’t know what the Surgeon General’s Daily Recommended Intake of Friendship should be, or how it might vary from person to person. We don’t know what our social-stats are actually targeting—is it words spoken, whites of eyes seen, or some other, hyper-dimensional construct that would make no sense to our conscious minds? And we don’t know how those critical social nutrients actually make it into the system. Why is it hard to leave an all-you-can-eat buffet feeling hungry, but easy to leave a party feeling lonely?

Fortunately, we do know three things. First, whatever it is that keeps our minds from slime-ifying, you can’t get all of it from remote interactions. During the pandemic, I had plenty of Zooms, plenty of texting and phone calls and _Call of Duty_ with the dudes, and I still got social scurvy. To achieve healthy levels of social stimulation, you need face time, not just FaceTime.

Second, we know that you can’t get your social nourishment from intimates alone. If complete social isolation is like smoking unfiltered cigarettes, then only talking to the folks in your household is like vaping—better, but not good for you. A healthy social diet means occasionally conversing with people who share neither your genes nor your mailing address.

And third, we know that although people are unreasonably negative about their social interactions, we can at least partially counteract this bias. Over and over again, [studies find](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/15298868.2020.1816568) that people think that their past conversations went worse than they actually did and that future conversations will go worse than they actually do. But when you just make people talk to each other, [they end up having a nice time and feeling more confident about their conversational abilities](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022103122000750).

That suggests the best prescription for an inadequate social-stat is a bit of brute force. Just as you must sometimes drink even when you’re not thirsty, you must sometimes hang out even when you’re not lonely. As Kurt Vonnegut [put it in a commencement address in 1978](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/05/12/kurt-vonnegut-if-this-isnt-nice-fredonia/):

> I recommend that everybody here join all sorts of organizations, no matter how ridiculous, simply to get more people in his or her life. It does not matter much if all the other members are morons. Quantities of relatives of any sort are what we need.

I know why we’re so willing to opt out of hanging out—I mean, have you _seen_ people? Do you know what they’re capable of? Every hurt, every heartbreak and letdown you’ve ever had, you best believe there’s a _homo sapiens_ on the other side of it. There is no safe level of exposure to our species. So why not keep them at bay if you can?

I suppose because [the things that make you crazy are the only things you’ll ever truly love](https://www.experimental-history.com/p/thank-you-for-being-annoying). We evolved to tangle with each other, and we shrivel up and die if we don’t. Hell is other people? No way man. Hell is when your teeth fall out because nobody was there to remind you to eat an orange.

The cybernetic model of psychology says that we get hits of happiness for re-aligning our control systems, and the bigger the correction, the greater the pleasure. That may be why asphyxiation is so often preceded by the word “erotic”, but I leave this as a matter for future research.

[4](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/there-is-no-epidemic-of-loneliness#footnote-anchor-4)

Here’s another example. All humans have an air-stat that causes them to freak out if they can’t breathe. The air-stat is one of the strongest control systems around—if someone’s squeezing your throat or you’ve been underwater for too long, every neuron you’ve got will be trying to figure out how to get a gulp of air. But it turns out that the air-stat is [much more sensitive](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10986303/) to the amount of carbon dioxide in the lungs than it is to the amount of oxygen. Historically, this was a fine proxy—if you’re not clearing your CO2, then something is clearly going wrong.

Recently, however, humans have invented ways to fiddle with the mix of gases around us, allowing us to adjust the level of oxygen without affecting the level of carbon dioxide. For instance, processing plants use liquid nitrogen to flash-freeze meat, and if that nitrogen leaks out, it’ll turn into gas that can displace the oxygen in the room. Because we are not as sensitive to insufficient oxygen levels or to excess nitrogen levels—the atmosphere is about [78%](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Earth) nitrogen anyway—if you find yourself in this situation, you might become disoriented, fall unconscious, asphyxiate, and die, all without your air-stat sounding the alarm. That’s what happened in Georgia in 2021: [six workers died](https://www.npr.org/2021/07/23/1019784347/six-poultry-workers-died-from-a-nitrogen-leak-osha-has-issued-1-million-in-fines) at a poultry processing plant when a freezer malfunctioned and started spewing nitrogen gas. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration [requires](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA4450.pdf) workplaces like these to deploy oxygen detectors precisely because humans do not come with those detectors preinstalled.

I’m familiar with this because a similar accident happened right outside my town shortly before I was born. A farmer entered a manure pit to try to clear a clog, but the methane fumes were so strong that he collapsed from a lack of oxygen. His brother came to rescue him and also collapsed. Sadly, [both died](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00001448.htm). My parents would tell me this story whenever we drove past the farm, and it’s stuck with me ever since.

[5](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/there-is-no-epidemic-of-loneliness#footnote-anchor-5)

You might wonder: isn’t this just a matter of introversion vs. extraversion? Is the problem just that everyone needs to be a bit more extraverted?

This is a reasonable hypothesis, but it mixes up two distinct concepts. In cybernetic psychology, people’s thermostats differ not only in their _set points_—the target level that each control system is trying to maintain—but also in their _sensitivities_, which is how quickly and vigorously those systems will fight to restore balance when things go out of whack. A big beefy dude needs to eat more food to stay alive than a petite old lady does (different set points), but they could feel equally hungry when they don’t get their respective amounts of necessary nutrition (same sensitivities). If you turn down the sensitivities on their food-stats, both of them could end up equally malnourished, even if the beefy guy is eating more than the old lady.

The same thing could happen socially. Extraverts may need more social “nutrition” than introverts do—that’s the difference in set points. But if their control systems aren’t sensitive enough—that is, if they don’t respond strongly enough when they fail to reach their set point—both of them could end up socially malnourished, even if the extravert is spending more time with other people overall.

Why would our water-intake control systems leave us slightly high and dry? I have a few guesses:

1.   Our evolutionary ancestors did not have constant and easy access to safe drinking water, so they needed to be able to [endure some amount of dehydration without their hydro-stats freaking out](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39304116/).

2.   Prehistoric foods probably contained more water than modern foods do (not a lot of crackers and Cheerios in the hunter-gatherer diet). So the food-stat was shouldering some of the hydro-stat’s burden.

3.   Ancient humans consumed [much less salt than we do today](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10922153/); their hydro-stats never had to contend with a tube of Pringles.
